newsitem.title: USA: White House economic adviser Tyson leaving.
newsitem.headline: White House economic adviser Tyson leaving.

text.p: White House economic adviser Laura Tyson, one of a handful of women in President Bill Clinton's inner circle, is leaving to teach at the University of California at Berkeley, her office said on Tuesday.

"She's leaving but she's willing to stay until the transition (to Clinton's second term) is complete," Tyson's spokesman Christopher Dorval said, indicating she would stay until January at the latest. Clinton will be inaugurated for his second term on Jan. 20.

For the last two years Tyson chaired Clinton's National Economic Council, which coordinates administration economic policies. Before that she headed the Council of Economic Advisers, which analyses economic trends and makes forecasts.
During her tenure the economy expanded steadily, pushing unemployment down to its lowest levels in about 7 1/2 years.

Tyson, 49, joined a relatively large exodus from the top ranks of the Clinton administration as it prepared for another four years in office. Six Cabinet secretaries and White House chief of staff Leon Panetta were said to be leaving.

Dorval said he did not know when Tyson's successor would be named or who it might be but assumed he or she would work with Tyson for a time before she leaves. Meanwhile Tyson was working on "a series of transition items," Dorval said.
These included studying whether to form commissions to reform Medicare and Social Security, the government health care and pension plans for the elderly.

Dorval said Tyson was leaving for "only one reason: family." Her husband, screenwriter Erik Tarloff, and their 13-year-old son Elliot have already moved back to California, where the family lived before coming to Washington after Clinton's 1992 election victory.

Tyson was asked if she would be interested in any other Cabinet posts but she refused, Dorval said. She had made it no secret in Washington that she was unhappy with not being able to spend more time with her husband and son.

Tarloff adjusted to life in Washington by writing jokes for some of Clinton's speeches and penning amusing articles about what life was like as a Cabinet spouse, but he also flew back and forth to Los Angeles to keep up his contacts there.

Clinton named several women to high posts after he won the presidency in 1992 but as an adviser on the subject Clinton had made his top campaign priority, the economy, Tyson played an especially important role in his White House.

Her initial appointment to lead the Council of Economic Advisers was a surprise that drew fire from some economists, who disliked her ideas about an activist trade policy. But she established herself as a credible and frank adviser and an outspoken advocate of White House policies.
